procedural_history.originating_court: Metropolitan Magistrate -10, South-East, Saket Court (the “Trial Court”)
procedural_history.impugned_order: Order dated 03.08.2017 passed by the Metropolitan Magistrate summoning Mr. Amrit Sandhu Coaster/Respondent No. 2 in relation to the commission of an offence under Section 138 of the NI Act
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The High Court of Delhi, in CRL. M.C. No. 556 of 2019, passed an order dated 06.09.2022, quashing the order of the Metropolitan Magistrate. The High Court quashed the proceedings because it believed the underlying debt/liability was time-barred on the date the summoning order was issued.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The original complainant in the case lodged under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 appealed to the Supreme Court, assailing the High Court's order. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal and set aside the High Court's order, restoring the proceedings to the Trial Court.

directions: The Impugned Order is set aside.
The proceedings emanating from the Underlying Complaint i.e., CC No. 6437 of 2017 is restored to the file of the Trial Court.
Pending application(s), if any, are disposed of.

issue.issue_text: Whether the High Court, exercising its jurisdiction under Section 482 of the CrPC, is justified in quashing a summoning order in a Section 138 NI Act case on the premise that the underlying debt is time-barred.

facts: A Metropolitan Magistrate issued a summoning order against a person (Respondent No. 2) for an offence under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments (NI) Act.
The accused approached the High Court under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (CrPC) to quash this summoning order.

The High Court quashed the proceedings, reasoning that the underlying debt was time-barred. It based this conclusion on the fact that the original transaction occurred in 2011, while the cheque was issued in 2017, with no acknowledgment of the debt in the interim.
law: The Supreme Court referred to its precedent in *Yogesh Jain v. Sumesh Chadha*.
This precedent establishes that once a cheque is issued and dishonored, a statutory presumption arises under Sections 118 and 139 of the NI Act, which the accused must rebut through evidence.
The question of whether a cheque was issued for a time-barred debt is a matter of evidence.
application: The Court applied the legal principle from its precedent, stating that the issue of whether an underlying debt is barred by limitation is a "mixed question of law and fact."
Such a question must be decided based on evidence presented by both parties during a trial.
It is not a matter that can or should be decided by the High Court in a summary proceeding under Section 482 of the CrPC, which is not the appropriate forum for adjudicating on evidentiary matters.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the High Court's decision, holding that the High Court was not justified in quashing the summoning order. The question of whether the debt was time-barred is a triable issue that involves evidence and is a mixed question of law and fact, which should be decided by the trial court, not by the High Court exercising its jurisdiction under Section 482 CrPC.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the High Court, exercising its jurisdiction under Section 482 of the CrPC, is justified in quashing a summoning order in a Section 138 NI Act case on the premise that the underlying debt is time-barred.
appellant_arguments: The question of whether a cheque was issued for a time-barred debt is a matter of evidence that should be decided during the trial.
The High Court should not have adjudicated this factual issue in an application filed under Section 482 of the CrPC.
Once a cheque is issued and dishonored, a legal presumption arises under Sections 118 and 139 of the NI Act, which is for the accused to rebut at trial.
respondent_arguments: The underlying debt for which the cheque was issued was barred by limitation.
The transactions, including an Assured Returns Agreement and receipts, were from 2011, and there was no acknowledgment of the debt until the cheque was issued in 2017.
Since the debt was time-barred, it was not a 'legally enforceable debt or liability' as required under Section 138 of the NI Act, justifying the quashing of the proceedings.

cases.principle: Once a cheque is issued and dishonoured, it is for the accused to dislodge the legal presumption under Sections 118 and 139 of the NI Act. Whether the cheque was issued for a time-barred debt is a matter of evidence and cannot be adjudicated in an application under Section 482 of the CrPC.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: The question of whether an underlying debt or liability in a proceeding under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act is barred by limitation is a mixed question of law and fact which must be decided by the trial court based on evidence and cannot be adjudicated by a High Court exercising its jurisdiction under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The classification of the underlying debt or liability as being barred by limitation is a question that must be decided based on the evidence adduced by the parties. The question regarding the time barred nature of an underlying debt or liability in proceedings under Section 138 of the NI Act is a mixed question of law and fact which ought not to be decided by the High Court exercising jurisdiction under Section 482 of the CrPC.
legal_tests_applied: Whether an issue constitutes a mixed question of law and fact that requires evidence and is therefore unsuitable for adjudication in a summary proceeding under Section 482 of the CrPC.

Application of the statutory presumption under Sections 118 and 139 of the NI Act, which arises upon the issuance and dishonor of a cheque, and places the burden on the accused to rebut it with evidence at trial.
why_appellant_lost: The respondent's argument that the debt was time-barred was rejected as a basis for quashing the proceedings under Section 482 CrPC because this determination is a matter of evidence.

The High Court's reliance on documents like an agreement and receipts from 2011 to conclude the debt was time-barred was an improper adjudication of a mixed question of law and fact that should have been left for trial.
why_respondent_won: Once a cheque is issued and dishonored, a statutory presumption arises under Sections 118 and 139 of the NI Act, which is for the Accused to dislodge through evidence at trial.

Whether the cheque in question had been issued for a time barred debt or not, itself prima facie, is a matter of evidence and could not have been adjudicated in an application filed by the Accused Under Section 482 of the CrPC.
policy_considerations: The jurisdiction under Section 482 of the CrPC should not be exercised to adjudicate mixed questions of law and fact, as this would amount to conducting a mini-trial and usurping the role of the trial court, which is the proper forum for evaluating evidence.
